claim: The eLife Features team has summarized over 2,400 articles in plain language.
source: After summarizing over 2,400 articles in plain language, the eLife Features team shares what it has learnt about writing and editing for a broad audience.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual count of articles summarized.

claim: eLife digests are part of a wider effort to make original research as open and accessible as possible.
source: Firstly, we see digests as part of a wider effort to make original research as open and accessible as possible.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the purpose and positioning of eLife digests within broader accessibility efforts.

claim: Anyone with an Internet connection can freely read articles published in eLife.
source: Being an open-access journal means that anyone (with an Internet connection) can freely read articles published in eLife.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the accessibility of eLife articles based on the journal's open-access model.

claim: eLife digests help foster interdisciplinary research.
source: Secondly, eLife is a journal with a broad scope and eLife digests are one small way that we can help to foster interdisciplinary research.
evidence: This is a stated goal of the eLife digests program.

claim: A plant biologist with decades of experience in research is unlikely to also be an expert in neuroscience.
source: A plant biologist with decades of experience in research, for example, is unlikely to also be an expert in neuroscience (and vice versa).
evidence: This is presented as a general observation about scientific specialization.

claim: By working on an eLife digest, authors of the original research article gain skills and experience that can be applied to other situations.
source: By working on an eLife digest, the authors of the original research article gain skills and experience that can be applied to other situations.
evidence: This is stated as a benefit of the digest writing process for authors.

claim: Not every scientist gets formal training in communication skills.
source: However, not every scientist gets formal training in communication skills.
evidence: This is presented as a general observation about scientific training.

claim: eLife digests are handled by the Features editors who also look after Insights, interviews, podcasts and other magazine-style content in the journal.
source: Being aimed at a more general audience, the digests have always been handled by the Features editors who also look after Insights, interviews, podcasts and the other magazine-style content in the journal.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the organizational structure and responsibilities for digest production.

claim: Features editors and freelance writers write most eLife digests.
source: Together with some freelance writers, we write most eLife digests.
evidence: This is a direct statement about who writes the digests.

claim: Every digest is edited carefully and sent to the authors of the research paper for checking before it is published.
source: Every digest is edited carefully and sent to the authors of the research paper for checking before it is published
evidence: This describes the editorial process for digests.

claim: The Features team works closely with authors to ensure that each digest is a clear and accurate explanation of the main findings of their paper.
source: we work closely with the authors to ensure that each digest is a clear and accurate explanation of the main findings of their paper.
evidence: This describes the collaborative process between editors and authors.

claim: The challenge of writing an eLife digest is to explain the same concepts and findings as the paper but in language that most people would understand, without assuming that the reader has any previous specialist knowledge.
source: Instead the challenge is to explain the same concepts and findings as the paper but in language that most people would understand, and without assuming that the reader has any previous specialist knowledge.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the writing challenge for digests.

claim: The writing style in a digest should be more active and engaging than the passive and formal style that is characteristic of most scientific articles.
source: The writing style in a digest should also be more active and engaging than the passive and formal style that is characteristic of most scientific articles.
evidence: This is a stated guideline for digest writing style.

claim: A good eLife digest is clear, concise and complete.
source: Instead, a good eLife digest is clear, concise and complete
evidence: This is a direct statement of the qualities of a good digest.

claim: A good eLife digest states the facts without resorting to exaggeration or hype.
source: it states the facts without resorting to exaggeration or hype.
evidence: This is a stated principle for digest writing.

claim: Each eLife digest is published in a prominent position, immediately below the abstract of its research article.
source: Each eLife digest is published in a prominent position, immediately below the abstract of its research article.
evidence: This describes the placement of digests on the eLife website.

claim: The intended audience for eLife digests includes people who do not normally visit journal websites.
source: However, the intended audience also includes people who do not normally visit journal websites.
evidence: This is a stated goal about the target audience for digests.

claim: eLife regularly re-publishes some digests on Medium, a social publishing platform.
source: To reach more of these readers, we regularly re-publish some digests on Medium, a social publishing platform.
evidence: This describes a distribution strategy for digests.

claim: eLife has been publishing eLife digests for almost five years (as of the time of writing).
source: After almost five years of publishing eLife digests, what have we learnt about writing plain-language summaries?
evidence: This provides a timeframe for the digest program.

claim: You can write a digest for any research paper, including papers that would not typically attract the attention of the wider media.
source: We are confident that you can write a digest for any research paper, including papers that would not typically attract the attention of the wider media.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experience with the digest program.

claim: eLife has written digests about the discovery of Homo naledi.
source: Sure, we have written digests about the discovery of Homo naledi and how one in four shark species are on the brink of extinction.
evidence: This is a specific example of a digest topic.

claim: eLife has written digests about how one in four shark species are on the brink of extinction.
source: Sure, we have written digests about the discovery of Homo naledi and how one in four shark species are on the brink of extinction.
evidence: This is a specific example of a digest topic.

claim: eLife has written digests about how scuttle flies develop as embryos.
source: But we have also tackled topics like how scuttle flies develop as embryos, how proteins form changing patterns inside artificial chambers, and how sodium and potassium ions are pumped across cell membranes.
evidence: This is a specific example of a digest topic.

claim: eLife has written digests about how proteins form changing patterns inside artificial chambers.
source: But we have also tackled topics like how scuttle flies develop as embryos, how proteins form changing patterns inside artificial chambers, and how sodium and potassium ions are pumped across cell membranes.
evidence: This is a specific example of a digest topic.

claim: eLife has written digests about how sodium and potassium ions are pumped across cell membranes.
source: But we have also tackled topics like how scuttle flies develop as embryos, how proteins form changing patterns inside artificial chambers, and how sodium and potassium ions are pumped across cell membranes.
evidence: This is a specific example of a digest topic.

claim: Digests are especially valuable for papers that are unlikely to be highlighted in a press release or attract coverage in the media.
source: We feel that digests are especially valuable in such papers because they are unlikely to be highlighted in a press release or attract coverage in the media.
evidence: This is a stated opinion about the value of digests for certain types of papers.

claim: Providing regular feedback to freelance writers results in better drafts that require less editing and revision.
source: We have found, for example, that providing regular feedback to freelance writers results in better drafts that require less editing and revision.
evidence: This is a finding from the team's experience with the digest process.

claim: Most authors are willing to get involved in preparing an eLife digest for their paper if given the opportunity.
source: We have also found that most authors are willing to get involved in preparing an eLife digest for their paper if given the opportunity.
evidence: This is a finding from the team's experience with authors.

claim: Initially, the digests were written using the accepted manuscript and authors' cover letter as the primary sources of information.
source: Initially, the digests were written using the accepted manuscript and authors' cover letter as the primary sources of information.
evidence: This describes the original process for writing digests.

claim: In 2015, eLife started to think about how to involve the authors of the paper earlier in the process.
source: In 2015, we started to think about how we could involve the authors of the paper – who already knew all of these details – earlier in the process.
evidence: This describes a change in the digest preparation process.

claim: From May to July 2015, eLife ran a pilot study with 100 authors who had recently been invited to submit a revised manuscript.
source: From May to July 2015, we ran a pilot study with 100 authors who had recently been invited to submit a revised manuscript.
evidence: This describes a specific pilot study with dates and sample size.

claim: In the pilot study, 79 out of 100 authors sent answers to questions about key points for their digest.
source: This pilot study worked better than we had expected; most authors sent us some answers (79 out of 100), often before their manuscript had even been accepted.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the pilot study.

claim: Most authors in the pilot study sent answers before their manuscript had even been accepted.
source: This pilot study worked better than we had expected; most authors sent us some answers (79 out of 100), often before their manuscript had even been accepted.
evidence: This is an observation from the pilot study about timing of author responses.

claim: Most of the answers from authors in the pilot study were useful.
source: Importantly, most of the answers were useful.
evidence: This is an evaluation of the quality of author responses in the pilot study.

claim: Authors made fewer edits when checking their digests after the new process was implemented.
source: Authors also made fewer edits than before when checking their digests
evidence: This is a comparative observation about author behavior before and after the process change.

claim: eLife now asks authors to answer four questions to help write their digest.
source: and now we ask authors to answer four questions to help us write their digest.
evidence: This describes the current process for involving authors in digest preparation.

claim: Most authors underestimate how much they need to change their writing style to write for a non-specialist audience.
source: We also learnt that most authors underestimate how much they need to change their writing style to write for a non-specialist audience.
evidence: This is a finding from the team's experience working with authors.

claim: Being immersed in their research can make it harder for authors to write for people who do not know what they know, the so-called curse of knowledge.
source: This was not unexpected because we appreciate that being immersed in their research can make it harder for authors to write for people who do not know what they know, the so-called curse of knowledge.
evidence: This references a known cognitive phenomenon to explain author behavior.

claim: Giving clear instructions and breaking down the task by asking authors a few questions has been a good way to tap into their expert knowledge and write the digest more quickly.
source: Nevertheless, giving clear instructions and breaking down the task by asking authors a few questions has, in our experience, been a good way to tap into their expert knowledge and write the digest more quickly.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the team's experience about effective methods for working with authors.

claim: Refining the process helped eLife prepare digests for every paper even as the journal grew.
source: Refining the process helped us to prepare eLife digests for every paper even as the journal grew.
evidence: This describes the impact of process improvements on digest production capacity.

claim: By 2016, it was clear that writing a digest cannot be rushed.
source: By 2016, however, it was clear that writing a digest cannot be rushed.
evidence: This is a realization from the team's experience by a specific year.

claim: eLife made the decision to stop publishing a digest for every research article as the number of papers accepted each month continued to climb.
source: As the number of papers accepted each month continued to climb, we made the difficult decision to stop publishing a digest for every research article.
evidence: This describes a policy change in response to increasing publication volume.

claim: eLife now identifies a selection of about 60 papers each month for eLife digests.
source: Instead, we now identify a selection of about 60 papers each month for eLife digests.
evidence: This provides a quantitative description of the current digest production volume.

claim: Papers for digests are selected based on a range of criteria including author willingness, recommendations from the Board of Reviewing Editors, reader interest, and interdisciplinary potential.
source: These are selected based on a range of criteria: first and foremost, we want to offer digests to those authors who show the most willing to get involved early on in the process. Secondly, we rely on recommendations from eLife's Board of Reviewing Editors to find those papers that are the most significant within their fields. Lastly, we select other papers from areas that most interest our readers, and especially those papers that attempt to bridge different disciplines.
evidence: This describes the selection criteria for papers to receive digests.

claim: Well over 90% of authors tell eLife that they'd like to work with them to prepare an eLife digest for their paper.
source: What we do know is that well over 90% of authors tell us that they'd like to work with us to prepare an eLife digest for their paper.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about author interest in digests.

claim: When people read research articles on the eLife website each month, somewhere between 13% and 25% of the time they read the digest.
source: We also know that when people read research articles on the eLife website each month, somewhere between 13% and 25% of the time they read the digest.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about digest readership.

claim: Based on surveys, the current audience for digests is mainly scientists, though some non-scientists regularly read digests too.
source: Based on surveys, we know that the current audience is mainly scientists, though some non-scientists regularly read digests too.
evidence: This is a finding from survey data about the digest audience composition.

claim: Among scientists, there was a slight preference for reading digests in papers in their own field as opposed to other fields of research.
source: Among the scientists, there was a slight preference for reading digests in papers in their own field as opposed to other fields of research
evidence: This is a finding from survey data about scientist reading preferences.

claim: 93% of scientists who read digests in other fields found them useful.
source: but 93% of those who read digests in other fields found them useful.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from survey data about the perceived usefulness of digests.

claim: Scientists and non-scientists alike felt that more journals should consider providing plain-language summaries of research articles.
source: Lastly, scientists and non-scientists alike felt that more journals should consider providing plain-language summaries of research articles.
evidence: This is a finding from survey data about attitudes toward plain-language summaries.

claim: In the future, eLife will be looking to ask authors about their motivations, expectations and experience of writing plain-language summaries.
source: In the future, we'll be looking to ask authors about their motivations, expectations and experience of writing plain-language summaries.
evidence: This describes a planned future research direction.

claim: eLife will be increasing efforts to reach new audiences and make digests more discoverable in general.
source: In addition, we will be increasing our efforts to reach new audiences, and make digests more discoverable in general.
evidence: This describes planned future actions.
